steps.name: prompt

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
ADLs can be classified into three broad categories: informal box-and-line drawings, formal architecture description languages, and notations based on UML (unified modeling language).

For a long time box-and-line drawings have been the most predominant way of describing software architectures. They provide useful documentation, but because they are so informal this limited how useful the architecture description could be, and a more rigorous way of describing software architectures was needed. Allen and Garlan (1997) say: "while these [box-and-line] descriptions may provide useful documentation, the current level of informality limits their usefulness. Since it is generally imprecise what is meant by such architectural descriptions, it may be impossible to analyze an architecture for consistency or determine non-trivial properties of it. Moreover, there is no way to check that a system implementation is faithful to its architectural design." Perry and Wolf (1992) come to a similar conclusion, reporting that: "Aside from providing clear and precise documentation, the primary purpose of specifications is to provide automated analysis of the documents and to expose various kinds of problems that would otherwise go undetected."

Since then there has been a thread of research on formal languages for describing software architecture. Tens of formal ADLs have been proposed. Each one has different conceptual architectural elements, different syntax or semantics, focuses on a specific operational domain, or is only suitable for different analysis techniques. For example, there are domain-specific ADLs for embedded and real-time systems (such as AADL, EAST-ADL, and EADL), for control-loop applications (DiaSpec), for product line architectures (Koala), and for dynamic systems (Π-ADL). There are also analysis-specific ADLs for availability, reliability, security, resource consumption, data quality and real-time performance analysis (AADL), for behavioral analysis (Fractal), and for trustworthiness analysis (TADL).

- not the desired adoption in industrial practice
- reasons analysed by Woods and Hilliard, Pandey, Clements, others: rarely integrated in life-cycle, seldom mature tools, scarcely documented, very specific needs, no space for extensions
- UML indicated as possible successor of existing ADLs; many proposals to use/extend UML for software architectures
- 2013 study: practitioners generally satisfied with design capabilities; concerns: lacked analysis features and extra-functional properties; ADLs used in practice mostly from industry not academia; need more formality, better usability

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
ADLs can be classified into three broad categories: informal box-and-line drawings, formal architecture description languages, and notations based on UML (unified modeling language).

For a long time box-and-line drawings have been the most predominant way of describing software architectures. They provide useful documentation, but because they are so informal this limited how useful the architecture description could be, and a more rigorous way of describing software architectures was needed. Allen and Garlan (1997) say: "while these [box-and-line] descriptions may provide useful documentation, the current level of informality limits their usefulness. Since it is generally imprecise what is meant by such architectural descriptions, it may be impossible to analyze an architecture for consistency or determine non-trivial properties of it. Moreover, there is no way to check that a system implementation is faithful to its architectural design." Perry and Wolf (1992) come to a similar conclusion, reporting that: "Aside from providing clear and precise documentation, the primary purpose of specifications is to provide automated analysis of the documents and to expose various kinds of problems that would otherwise go undetected."

Since then there has been a thread of research on formal languages for describing software architecture. Tens of formal ADLs have been proposed. Each one has different conceptual architectural elements, different syntax or semantics, focuses on a specific operational domain, or is only suitable for different analysis techniques. For example, there are domain-specific ADLs for embedded and real-time systems (such as AADL, EAST-ADL, and EADL), for control-loop applications (DiaSpec), for product line architectures (Koala), and for dynamic systems (Π-ADL). There are also analysis-specific ADLs for availability, reliability, security, resource consumption, data quality and real-time performance analysis (AADL), for behavioral analysis (Fractal), and for trustworthiness analysis (TADL).

However, industrial practice has not adopted these efforts as much as was hoped. Woods and Hilliard, Pandey, Clements, and others have looked at some of the reasons why industry has not adopted them: formal ADLs have rarely been integrated in the software life-cycle, they are seldom supported by mature tools, they are scarcely documented, they focus on very specific needs, and they leave no space for extensions that would let new features be added.

To overcome some of these limitations, UML has been indicated as a possible successor to the existing ADLs. Many proposals have been made to use the UML or extend it so that it can model software architectures more properly.

A study from 2013 found that practitioners were generally satisfied with the design capabilities of the ADLs they used. But they had several major concerns with them: the ADLs lacked analysis features and the ability to define extra-functional properties; the ones used in practice mostly came from industrial development and not from academic research; and they needed more formality and better usability.
